webdavy.description: WebDavy is a Chrome browser extension based on the WebDAV protocol that allows you to manage remote file servers without leaving your browser. Whether it's personal cloud storage or enterprise file servers, WebDavy provides a convenient file management experience with support for uploading, downloading, browsing, and organizing files.

title.battery-killer: BatteryKiller - Battery Charge Cycling for macOS | Range-based Power Control - HolaTiger
apps.title: Desktop Apps
apps.subtitle: Native little tools that do one thing well and then sit quietly in the menu bar
battery-killer.name: BatteryKiller
battery-killer.desc: A macOS menu bar tool that cycles the battery inside a range you set, so the charge never sits at 100% for months on end.
battery-killer.description: BatteryKiller switches the MacBook power adapter on and off in software: the adapter is cut when the charge reaches the upper bound so the battery actually discharges, and restored at the lower bound so it charges again. On a Mac that stays plugged in as a desktop, the battery no longer sits pinned at 100%.
battery-killer.hero.title: cycles your battery inside a range you choose
battery-killer.features.title: What it does
battery-killer.features.subtitle: Range cycling, one-click power switching and a permanent menu bar presence — the charging rhythm goes back to you.
battery-killer.feature1.title: Automatic charge cycling
battery-killer.feature1.desc: The adapter is cut once the charge hits the upper bound so the battery genuinely discharges, then restored at the lower bound so it charges again. And so on.
battery-killer.feature2.title: One-click power source switch
battery-killer.feature2.desc: A single button flips between battery power and DC power, and stops a running cycle the moment you press it.
battery-killer.feature3.title: Two-handle cycle range
battery-killer.feature3.desc: Two handles set the discharge floor and the charge ceiling, snapping to 5 / 10 / 20 / 30 and 80 / 90 / 100 near those ticks. The range locks while a cycle is running.
battery-killer.feature4.title: Live status and phase
battery-killer.feature4.desc: A large charge percentage, the power state (charging / plugged in but idle / running on battery) and what the cycle is doing right now.
battery-killer.feature5.title: Always in the menu bar
battery-killer.feature5.desc: The icon follows the power source. The menu toggles the cycle, switches power and opens the window. Closing the window does not stop anything.
battery-killer.feature6.title: Bilingual, with safe exits
battery-killer.feature6.desc: The UI follows the system language and can be switched by hand. A power assertion is held while cycling so the Mac cannot idle-sleep, and the adapter is restored before quitting.
battery-killer.steps.title: Three steps to a cycling battery
battery-killer.steps.subtitle: Once installed, it is two handles and one switch.
battery-killer.step1.title: Download and install
battery-killer.step1.desc: Grab the dmg or zip from GitHub Releases and drag it into Applications. The app is unsigned and unnotarized, so the first launch needs a right-click → Open.
battery-killer.step2.title: Authorize once
battery-killer.step2.desc: The first time you hit Auto Cycle, enter your administrator password once to install the privileged helper. You are never asked again.
battery-killer.step3.title: Set a range and start
battery-killer.step3.desc: Drag the handles to pick a floor and a ceiling, flip Auto Cycle on, and let it run back and forth on its own.
battery-killer.screenshots.title: Screenshots
battery-killer.screenshots.subtitle: Every status and control lives in one window, with no extra layers.
battery-killer.gallery.item1.label: Chinese UI
battery-killer.gallery.item1.title: Charge, power state and cycle range
battery-killer.gallery.item1.desc: The large readout shows the charge and where power comes from, the button below switches source, two handles set the floor and ceiling, and the footer explains the current phase.
battery-killer.gallery.item2.label: English UI
battery-killer.gallery.item2.title: Follows your system language
battery-killer.gallery.item2.desc: Chinese locales get Chinese, everything else English. You can also switch it by hand from the window footer or the menu bar menu, and the choice is remembered.
battery-killer.tech.title: How it works
battery-killer.tech.subtitle: There is no public API for this, so it takes the SMC firmware plus a minimal privileged helper.
battery-killer.tech1.title: Power is controlled by the SMC key CHIE
battery-killer.tech1.desc: macOS exposes no public way to cut the charger; the real switch lives in the AppleSMC firmware. Writing CHIE = 0x00 enables the adapter, CHIE = 0x08 cuts it and the Mac runs on battery.
battery-killer.tech2.title: SMC writes need root, so there is a helper
battery-killer.tech2.desc: A non-root process can read SMC, but every write is rejected by the kernel. The helper bkhelper is kept alive by launchd as root and understands exactly four commands: VERSION / STATUS / ON / OFF.
battery-killer.tech3.title: Every write is read back and verified
battery-killer.tech3.desc: The SMC firmware sometimes reports success without applying the change, so every write is immediately read back and compared before it counts.
battery-killer.tech.note: Note: CHIE only expresses the intent of the power path — it does not mean the charger is physically attached, which is what AC-W or the IOKit power source API tell you. The app is built on a private SMC key, so a firmware update may change the behaviour. Use at your own risk.
battery-killer.usecases.title: Who it is for
battery-killer.usecases.subtitle: If your MacBook spends most of its life plugged in, this is for you.
battery-killer.usecase1: Desk-bound MacBooks: it stays plugged in as a desktop, and you would rather the charge did not sit at 100% year round.
battery-killer.usecase2: Battery health worriers: you want to avoid the swelling and capacity loss that come from months at full charge — without draining the battery to empty either.
battery-killer.usecase3: People who need to unplug on demand: flip to battery power with one click, to compare power draw or to burn some charge before heading out.
battery-killer.usecase4: Minimalists: you want one quiet menu bar tool, not a battery suite with a pile of background services.
battery-killer.faq.title: FAQ
battery-killer.faq.subtitle: Common questions about installation, permissions and supported Macs.
battery-killer.faq1.question: Which Macs does BatteryKiller support?
battery-killer.faq1.answer: Apple Silicon (arm64) Macs running macOS 13 or later. Intel Macs are not supported. It also only works on machines where the SMC key CHIE exists and is writable — anywhere else the app reports "This Mac does not support software control of the power adapter" at launch. That probe only reads SMC metadata, needs no root, and so never triggers a pointless authorization prompt.
battery-killer.faq2.question: Why does macOS say the developer cannot be verified?
battery-killer.faq2.answer: The project has no Apple Developer signature and is not notarized, so release builds are ad-hoc signed and Gatekeeper stops the first launch. Right-click → Open, or run xattr -rd com.apple.quarantine /Applications/BatteryKiller.app first. That is the state of the project, not a broken download — and it applies again after every update.
battery-killer.faq3.question: Why does it ask for an administrator password the first time?
battery-killer.faq3.answer: SMC writes must happen as root, while the GUI process always runs as the logged-in user. The app installs the privileged helper bkhelper into /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools and hands it to launchd, so you authorize exactly once and are never prompted again.
battery-killer.faq4.question: Will this damage the battery?
battery-killer.faq4.answer: Keeping the charge bouncing inside a range instead of parked at full is the friendlier pattern, and the two bounds are independent thresholds, so a charge hovering at one of them cannot flap. That said, it is built on a private SMC key, so a firmware update may change the behaviour. Use at your own risk.
battery-killer.faq5.question: What happens to power when I quit the app?
battery-killer.faq5.answer: The adapter is restored before the app exits, so the Mac is never left unplugged by accident. While a cycle is running it also holds a power assertion, so the machine cannot idle-sleep and freeze the loop.
battery-killer.faq6.question: Does it upload any of my data?
battery-killer.faq6.answer: No. It only reads battery state and talks to the SMC on your machine. No network access, no telemetry, and the source is public on GitHub.
